text: Sonam Wangchuk, born on 1 September 1966 in near Alchi, Leh district of Jammu and Kashmir (now in the Union Territory of Ladakh), is an Indian activist, innovator, education reformer, and environmentalist. He was not enrolled in school until the age of 9, as there were no schools in his village, and his mother taught him the basics in his mother tongue. In 1975, his father, Sonam Wangyal, became a minister in the Jammu and Kashmir Government. At age 9, Wangchuk was enrolled in a school in Srinagar, where he faced mistreatment due to his appearance, being addressed in a language he did not understand, which led to him being wrongly perceived as stupid. Unable to bear this, he escaped to Delhi in 1977 and pleaded with the school principal at a Kendriya Vidyalaya. He completed his B.Tech. in Mechanical Engineering from National Institute of Technology Srinagar (then REC Srinagar) in 1987, financing his education independently after a disagreement with his father over his engineering stream. He later pursued two years of higher studies in Earthen Architecture at Craterre School of Architecture in Grenoble, France, in 2011. In 1988, Wangchuk, along with his brother and five peers, founded the Students' Educational and Cultural Movement of Ladakh (SECMOL), which began experimenting with school reforms at the government high school in Saspol, leading to the launch of Operation New Hope in 1994 in collaboration with the government education department and village communities. From June 1993 to August 2005, he served as the editor of Ladakh's only print magazine, Ladags Melong. In 2001, he was appointed an education advisor to the Hill Council Government; in 2002, he co-founded the Ladakh Voluntary Network (LVN) and served as its secretary until 2005. He was part of the Drafting Committee for the Ladakh Hill Council Government’s Vision Document Ladakh 2025, which was formally launched by Prime Minister Manmohan Singh in 2005, and in 2005, he was appointed a member of the National Governing Council for Elementary Education in the Ministry of Human Resource Development, Government of India. From 2007 to 2010, he worked as an education advisor for MS, a Danish NGO. In late 2013, Wangchuk invented and built a prototype of the Ice Stupa, an artificial glacier that stores winter stream water in cone-shaped ice heaps, releasing it during late spring when farmers need it most. By the end of February 2014, his team had constructed a two-storey prototype capable of storing about 150,000 litres of water. In 2015, during a landslide that blocked the Phugtal river and created a 15 km long lake in Zanskar, Wangchuk proposed using a siphon technique and water jet erosion to safely drain the lake, but his advice was ignored, and blasting proceeded, leading to a flash flood on 7 May 2015 that destroyed 12 bridges and many fields. In 2016, he applied the Ice Stupa technique for disaster mitigation at high-altitude glacier lakes, leading a three-week expedition to South Lhonak Lake in Sikkim, installing a siphoning system to reduce the lake’s level. In late 2016, he was invited by the municipality of Pontresina, Switzerland, to build Ice Stupas as winter tourism attractions, and in October 2016, his team began constructing the first Ice Stupa in Europe with Swiss partners. In February 2018, local Ladakhi artists built a 10-foot-high ice stupa, completed in 25 days at around -12°C, housed within a larger ice tower. In February 2021, Wangchuk developed solar-powered tents for the Indian army, each accommodating about 10 soldiers, designed to trap daytime heat and retain warmth during the night, responding to the needs of around 50,000 soldiers working in harsh high-altitude conditions. In 2013, on student requests, he launched the New Ladakh Movement (NLM), a social campaign aimed at promoting sustainable education, environment, and economy, eventually becoming a non-political movement. In June 2020, in response to India-China border skirmishes at Galwan, he urged Indians to boycott Chinese products, a call that received widespread media coverage and celebrity support. On 26 January 2023, Wangchuk attempted a fast at Khardungla pass to highlight climate change impacts and demand protection for Ladakh under the Sixth Schedule of the Indian Constitution, but authorities allegedly prevented him from reaching the pass by placing him under house arrest, citing unsuitable temperatures below -40°C; the Ladakh police denied the charges. In March 2024, he initiated a fast-unto-death to demand constitutional safeguards for Ladakh and protection from industrial and mining activities, and began a 21-day Climate Fast for Ladakh’s statehood under the Sixth Schedule. On 30 September 2024, during a foot march from Ladakh to Delhi, he and supporters were detained by Delhi Police at the Singhu border and released on 2 October 2024. On 24 September 2025, a protest in Leh resulted in the burning of the BJP office and vandalism of the Ladakh Hill Council premises, leading to a police crackdown that killed four civilians and injured dozens, with a curfew imposed and mass arrests conducted. The Ministry of Home Affairs blamed Wangchuk for inciting the protests, which he denied, stating the protests reflected public frustration with the government. Two days later, on 2 October 2025, Wangchuk was detained by hundreds of police officers, led by the Ladakh Director General of Police, under the National Security Act (NSA). Internet services were suspended in Leh, and a curfew continued. Despite no formal detention order being issued to his family, Wangchuk was moved to Jodhpur Central Jail. The Home Ministry accused SECMOL of accepting dubious foreign funds and revoked its FCRA licence, while the CBI opened an inquiry into HIAL, and CRPF personnel were deployed against it. His wife, Gitanjali J Angmo, claimed the Ladakh DGP falsely accused Wangchuk of having "Pakistani links" because he attended a Himalayan Climate Convention in Pakistan in February with her, organized by the United Nations and Dawn Media, and was denied information about his health or condition, with authorities refusing her access to him. On 2 October, Angmo filed a Habeas corpus petition before the Supreme Court to challenge Wangchuk’s arrest. Wangchuk gained national attention in 2009 when his story inspired Aamir Khan’s character Phunsukh Wangdu in the film 3 Idiots, leading to him being referred to as "The real life Phunsukh Wangdu," though he has disavowed the comparison. Wangchuk is also known for designing the SECMOL campus, which runs on solar energy and uses no fossil fuels for cooking, lighting, or heating. His innovative contributions to Ladakh’s education and climate challenges have earned him numerous accolades, including the Ramon Magsaysay Award (2018), the title of Eminent Technologist of the Himalayan Region by IIT Mandi (2018), and the Global Award for Sustainable Architecture (2017), with around 15 awards as of 2025. He founded the Himalayan Institute of Alternatives Ladakh (HIAL) in 2015 with Gitanjali J Angmo, motivated by the need to address Ladakh’s unique geographical and cultural educational and developmental challenges, continuing his commitment to educational reform through HIAL, aiming to provide higher education and equip youth with skills for sustainable living in their environment. He has also designed and overseen the construction of several passive solar mud buildings in Ladakh, Sikkim, and Nepal, which remain warm even in winter temperatures as low as -30°C. In July 2016, SECMOL won the International Terra Award for the best building at the 12th World Congress on Earthen Architecture in Lyon, France, for its rammed earth 'Big Building' constructed using traditional, low-cost techniques and passive solar principles.
